name: Kite
note: A framed silk or linen panel tied to cordage is humanity's first controlled aerofoil. Rome has all materials. The curved bow of a framed kite's sides produces lift from asymmetric air flow; this was never trivial to understand. Kites serve tethered observation, signalling and scientific experiment.

name: Tethered observation balloon
note: A single large envelope of stitched linen or silk, sealed with beeswax, displaces enough warm air to lift a man. Must be tethered to cordage or risk becoming uncontrolled. The State values this for reconnaissance, signalling and military observation. A man in the sky appears miraculous; mitigation is training and controlled small-scale trials, not secrecy.

name: hot_air_balloon
note: Reference technology already in vocabulary. Hot air balloon relies on density difference: warm air inside the envelope is lighter than ambient air. Foundation for all free balloons.

name: Goldbeater's skin envelope
note: Goldbeater's skin, the cleaned intestine of oxen, is the best gas-tight material known. Thin, tough, airtight when sealed with alum and honey. Costs vastly more than linen but holds hydrogen. No rubber exists. This is the single choice for long-endurance gas bags.

name: Varnished silk envelope
note: Multiple coats of shellac varnish on silk create an airtight seam-sealed envelope. Much cheaper than goldbeater's skin, almost as airtight. Handles thermal stress better than intestine. This is the practical choice for large balloons when cost matters.

name: Hydrogen from iron and acid
note: Dilute sulfuric acid (from distillation) reacts with iron to produce hydrogen gas. Must be generated in sealed vessels with a tube fed to the envelope. Dangerous: hydrogen ignites explosively in air. Filling a balloon takes hours. This is the reliable source until coal gas is available. Rate is limited by acid strength and temperature control.

name: Coal gas for ballooning
note: Destructive distillation of coal produces a mixture rich in hydrogen and methane: coal gas. Vastly cheaper than chemical hydrogen. A coal-gas plant can fill balloons continuously. Requires establishing a permanent retort house and managing by-products. The lift is slightly less than pure hydrogen but the cost difference is transformative.

name: Balloon valve
note: A rope-pulled valve at the balloon's crown vents gas, allowing descent. Without it, a free balloon cannot descend safely. The valve must be airtight when closed but operate smoothly when pulled. A cone of leather over an iron frame, sealing under the weight of gas, is the only control a balloon has besides dropping ballast.

name: Ballast and descent control
note: A balloon achieves altitude by dropping sand ballast and descends by venting gas. These are its only two controls. Altitude is controlled by these two levers exclusively. A ballast bag with a line to the basket lets the aeronaut modulate buoyancy by hand.

name: Parachute
note: A cone of stiff linen attached to a harness. When opened in free fall, it spreads and catches air, slowing descent to survivable speeds. Requires both invention and extraordinary nerve to test. A man who falls from the sky with a cloth and lives appears either blessed or damned. The key insight is that air resistance, not upward force, saves you.

name: Elongated balloon envelope
note: Instead of a sphere, make the envelope elongated, pointed at both ends. This shape reduces drag hugely when the balloon drifts. The envelope must still be sealed and symmetrical. This is the form needed for a dirigible: long, narrow, and pointed.

name: Mounted engine under balloon
note: Suspend a small petrol engine and propeller in a wooden framework below an elongated envelope. The propeller drives air backward, creating thrust. The envelope provides lift. Requires a very light engine relative to power output and extreme care in weight balance. This is a dirigible, controllable by the pilot.

name: Rigid airship frame
note: Instead of one envelope, build a rigid skeleton of wooden rings and longerons, then cover with fabric and fill with gas. This allows huge structures and multiple gas cells for safety. Requires aluminium or steel girders to keep weight manageable. The Zeppelin approach: rigid frame, gasbags inside, and structural load is borne by the frame, not the envelope.

name: Hydrogen safety limits
note: Hydrogen is extraordinarily buoyant but ignites violently with air. A spark, a flame, static electricity, or friction will ignite any mixture between 4 percent and 75 percent hydrogen in air. This is not anecdotal: it is absolute chemistry. You cannot escape it by procedure; you mitigate by isolation (no open flames, grounding, no sparking equipment) and by accept that the risk is real and permanent. Helium does not exist. Coal gas is safer by dilution.

name: Cambered aerofoil section
note: Cayley's central discovery: a curved (cambered) plate lifts far better than a flat plate at the same angle of attack. The reason is non-obvious and requires experiment: curved surfaces create lower pressure on the back side. A wing with a cambered section can generate substantial lift at shallow angles. This is not merely a geometry trick; it is the foundation of mechanical flight.

name: Separation of forces: lift, drag, thrust, control
note: Cayley's single most important insight: lift and drag are separate. To fly, you need lift enough to equal weight, drag small enough that power can overcome it, thrust strong enough to overcome drag and accelerate, and control to direct the craft. These four are independent problems. Before Cayley, people treated flying as one vague problem. After him, it became engineering.

name: Wind tunnel for lift and drag measurement
note: A wooden box with a powerful fan at one end and a test section. Measurement is done with a water manometer: a bent tube of glass half-filled with water, showing pressure difference as height difference. You can test aerofoil shapes, measure lift and drag without dying. This is the tool that transforms flight from experiment to engineering. Build it first, use it to learn, then design based on data.

name: Simple glider
note: Build a wooden frame, cover with linen, add cambered wings and a tail. Tow it behind a horse or launch it downhill. It will glide and may kill the pilot if control is lost. But gliding flight teaches you what lift feels like, what turns require, and most importantly, what happens when you lose control. This is the cheap school, conducted at non-fatal altitudes.

name: Three-axis control: roll, pitch, yaw
note: The pilot must control three independent axes: roll (banking), pitch (nose up or down), and yaw (turning). Roll is achieved by wing warping or ailerons, pitch by elevator, yaw by rudder. A glider without all three controls is uncontrollable. Testing this kills people. But the Wright brothers realized that CONTROL, not lift or power, was the missing piece.

name: Wing warping
note: Twist the entire wing by pulling cables to alter the angle of attack at wing tips. This causes differential lift and forces the aircraft to roll. No moving surfaces are needed; the wing itself twists. This is elegant and strong, but requires great care in cable routing and tensioning. The Wright brothers used this. It works.

name: Aileron for roll control
note: Small hinged surfaces at the wing trailing edge, operated by pilot cables. When one goes up, the other goes down, creating differential lift without twisting the main wing. Simpler than warping and less stressful on structure. The aileron is a later refinement, but does the same job.

name: Rudder for yaw control
note: A hinged vertical fin at the tail. When deflected, it yaws the aircraft left or right. Essential for turning when wing warping or ailerons are used. Without it, the aircraft will slip sideways during a turn.

name: Elevator for pitch control
note: A hinged horizontal surface at the tail. When deflected up, the tail rises, and the nose drops. Down elevator raises the nose. This control pitch. It is the most critical: pitch controls altitude, and loss of pitch control is fatal in seconds.

name: Propeller as rotating aerofoil
note: A propeller is not a screw pushing against air like a screw in water. It is a rotating wing. Each blade is an aerofoil twisted to increasing angle as you go outward. It generates lift in a rotating plane, and that lift acts as thrust. Design requires aerofoil theory and matching pitch to engine speed. Inefficiency at the tips limits diameter.

name: Light petrol engine
note: An aircraft engine must deliver high power per kilogram. This requires aluminium alloys for the crankcase, fine tolerances for bearings and pistons, and very high speeds (1000 rpm+). A typical aero engine in 1910 delivered 10-30 horsepower at 200 kg. This is a metallurgy and precision problem first, a thermodynamics problem second.

name: Power-to-weight ratio and flight
note: A powered airplane needs enough power to overcome drag at the speed where wings produce lift sufficient for the weight. This requires roughly 5 to 10 kg of aircraft per horsepower. Achieving this needs an engine weighing very little per horsepower and an airframe weighing little. Both are metallurgy and precision problems, not power problems. Weak engines cannot overcome this limit regardless of design.

name: Powered aeroplane
note: An aircraft with engine and propeller that achieves sustained powered flight. Requires cambered wings tested in a wind tunnel, three-axis control, a light high-revving engine, and a structure so light it feels built from nothing. Testing kills the pilot. Only possible if all prerequisites are honest. The Wright brothers succeeded because they honored this checklist.

name: Radial engine
note: Cylinders arranged radially around a central crankshaft. Air cooling is excellent, and the engine is compact. Most effective for aircraft because the short length and small diameter reduce drag. Requires precise balancing and very strong crankshafts to handle the unbalanced forces.

name: Rotary engine
note: The entire engine block rotates with the propeller while the crankshaft stays fixed. The piston heads are cooled by rotation. High power at low weight. Much more complex than radial but delivers slightly better power. Used extensively in WWI aircraft. Requires very careful design to handle gyroscopic forces.

name: Biplane structure
note: Two main lifting surfaces separated vertically, braced together with struts and wire cables. This is strong, stiff, and light. All early aircraft were biplanes because they could be built from wood and wire. Drag is slightly higher than a monoplane, but the structural advantage is decisive when materials are weak.

name: Monoplane cantilever wing
note: One wing, supported only at the fuselage, with no external bracing. This requires a wing strong enough to cantilever its own load in bending. Needs steel or aluminium spars and good materials science to avoid failure. Much less drag than biplane, but much more demanding structurally. Not practical until materials improve.

name: Stressed-skin fuselage
note: Instead of a skeleton covered with skin, build the skin to carry bending loads. Aluminium sheet riveted to aluminium frames creates a strong, light, rigid structure. Requires precision sheet-metal work and tens of thousands of rivets. The monocoque: a form where the outer surface is the structure. This is how modern aircraft are built.

name: Airspeed indicator
note: A pitot tube measures dynamic pressure, which is velocity squared. Display it on a dial. A pilot cannot fly safely by feel; speed is invisible. This is the most important instrument. Early versions used a simple gauge; later ones an anemometer-style rotor. Without it, powered flight is nearly impossible.

name: Pitot tube
note: A simple tube with an opening into the airstream and a side port. Dynamic pressure at the front is higher than static pressure at the side. The difference is proportional to velocity squared. This is purely fluid statics, not magic.

name: Altimeter (aneroid barometer)
note: An aneroid capsule responds to atmospheric pressure. As altitude increases, pressure drops, the capsule expands slightly, and a mechanical linkage moves a dial. Needs to be calibrated carefully and compensated for temperature. Essential for instrument flying; a pilot cannot judge altitude reliably by eye.

name: Compass for navigation
note: A magnetized iron needle on a silk thread points north. Rome has this. A compass in an aircraft allows navigation when landmarks are obscured. Mount it in a card marked with degrees.

name: Artificial horizon (gyroscopic)
note: A rapidly spinning gyroscope maintains its orientation regardless of aircraft motion. Mount a ball or card inside the gyroscope's frame so the pilot sees whether wings are level and nose is up or down. Requires extreme precision in bearing design and high spin speeds. Essential for flying through clouds or darkness.

name: Flying boat
note: An aircraft whose fuselage is a boat hull. No need for an aerodrome; water launches are smooth and the hull provides flotation. Useful for long-range reconnaissance and transport. Requires excellent hydrodynamic design to minimize drag on the step and excellent corrosion control.

name: Aerodrome (landing field)
note: An open field of level ground, grass or gravel, at least 500 meters long and 100 meters wide. Aircraft need room to take off into wind and to land without hitting obstacles. A brick or gravel surface prevents mud. Early aerodromes were called flying grounds. They must be maintained and guarded.

name: Aerial photography
note: Mount a camera on an aircraft and photograph the ground below. Vertical photographs from height show cities, fields, fortifications with complete clarity and no perspective distortion. Absolutely invaluable for military reconnaissance and mapping. The camera must be light and the aircraft must be stable.

name: Aerial reconnaissance
note: An aircraft with a trained observer flies over enemy territory, notes positions of troops and defenses, and reports back. The observer is fast, covering in hours what a scout takes weeks to do. The State will fund this immediately. Requires pilot and observer to work in concert and to return safely.

name: Aerial bombing
note: Drop bombs from an aircraft onto targets below. Early bombs were heavy artillery shells with impact fuses. Later, purpose-designed bombs with light cases and heavy charges. Extremely dangerous for the pilot (instability, wind drift, primitive aiming). Devastatingly effective against stationary targets. The State will demand this.

name: Helicopter rotor system
note: Two or more large aerofoil blades rotating at high speed about a vertical axis. The blades generate lift and must be able to change pitch to control thrust direction. This is mechanically complex and unstable without careful design. A helicopter can hover and land vertically, but is harder to fly than an airplane.

name: Autogyro (powered rotor-wing)
note: A propeller on the nose for forward thrust, and a rotor overhead spinning freely (autogiro: self-turning). As the aircraft moves forward, air flowing through the rotor keeps it spinning, generating lift. Simpler than a helicopter because the rotor needs no engine drive, only control linkages. Can take off and land in short distances. Invented much later than the helicopter.

name: Jet engine principle
note: Newton's third law: jet out the back, thrust forward. A compressor forces air in, fuel burns in a combustion chamber, hot gas expands and exits at high velocity. No piston engine, no propeller. Much simpler mechanically than reciprocating engines but requires materials that survive continuous high temperature under pressure.

name: Jet engine (centrifugal compressor)
note: A centrifugal compressor spins at thousands of rpm, sucking air in at the center and throwing it outward into a combustion chamber. The challenge is not compression but surviving high temperature. Combustion temperatures are 1000C+, and metal strength drops catastrophically above 600C. Nickel alloys are essential. Even then, turbine blades fail unless cooled internally.
